Mausoleum|mark={{ill|Octagonal Kofun|ja|八角墳}}.svg|marksize=28|caption=|position=bottom|width=200|float=center}} }} '''Kengoshizuka Kofun''' is a [[Kofun]] in [[Asuka, Nara]] Japan.Tokuse, Takahiko, and Eriko Oka. "Life in Archaeological Sites and Settlements in Asuka Village as a Model Case for Managing Settlements Adjacent to Archaeological Sites: A Proposal for the Future of Saqqara." The journal of Center for the Global Study of Cultural Heritage and Culture 2 (2015): 5-20.{{cite book |title=Burial Mounds in Europe and Japan: Comparative and Contextual Perspectives |date=30 September 2018 |doi=10.2307/j.ctv1228gf7|s2cid=240193791 }} Specifically, it is an [[Octagonal Kofun]]. It is said to be the burial site of [[Empress Kōgyoku]].{{Cite web |title=Kengoshizuka Kofun Tumulus, Koshitsuka-gomon Kofun Tumulus |url=http://asuka-japan-heritage.jp/global/en/saimei/detail/kengosiduka_sa.html |access-date=2023-10-20 |website=Exploring the Footsteps of the Heroines of Asuka |language=en}}{{Cite news |date=2022-03-04 |title=Octagonal burial mound said to belong to ancient Japan empress reconstructed in Nara Pref. |language=en |work=Mainichi Daily News |url=https://mainichi.jp/english/articles/20220304/p2a/00m/0na/040000c |access-date=2023-10-20}} it was reconstructed and opened to the public on May 6 2022. This contrasts with other Imperial tombs such as the [[Mausoleum of Emperor Tenji]] which are closed to the public by the [[Imperial Household Agency]].{{Cite web |title=Gobyōyama Kofun (in Kyōto) - Passage Grave in Japan in Honshū |url=https://www.megalithic.co.uk/article.php?sid=33021 |access-date=2023-10-21 |website=The Megalithic Portal}} [[File:220311 Kengoshiduka 3.jpg|thumb|Entrance to the burial chamber]] ==overview== '''Kengoshizuka Kofun''' (牽牛子塚古墳) is a {{ill|Kofun|ja|古墳}} located in {{ill|Asuka, Nara|ja|明日香村}}, {{ill|Nara Prefecture|ja|奈良県}}, Japan. It is an {{ill|Octagonal Kofun|ja|八角墳}} and has been designated as a National Historic Site. The excavated artifacts from the site are designated as National Important Cultural Properties. The name "Kengoshizuka" includes the word "{{ill|Asagao|ja|アサガオ}}" ([[:en:Ipomoea_nil|Morning Glory]]), an alternate reading for "Kengoshi." The tumulus is also referred to as "Omae-zuka."[http://www.asukamura.jp/chosa_hokoku/kengoshizuka/kengoshizuka.html Kengoshizuka Kofun] Asuka Village Official Website Excavations conducted between 2009 and 2010 revealed that the tumulus was octagonal, strengthening its association with {{ill|Empress Saimei|ja|斉明天皇}}, mother of {{ill|Emperor Tenji|ja|天智天皇}} and {{ill|Emperor Tenmu|ja|天武天皇}}. Full restoration was completed in February 2022.Nara's Asuka Morning Glory Kofun fully restored, "Mainichi Shimbun," March 3, 2022, Osaka Morning Edition == location == The tumulus is located near the border of {{ill|Kashihara|ja|橿原市}} and lies at the stable, broad apex of a hill in {{ill|Asuka, Nara|ja|明日香村}}. Its summit reaches an elevation of 126.3 meters and is approximately 500 meters west of the {{ill|Iwayayama Kofun|ja|岩屋山古墳}}, another National Historic Site. == Exterior and Scale == The site was previously known for its unique internal structure, consisting of two hollowed chambers within a massive stone. This led to theories that it served as a combined tomb for Empress Saimei and her daughter {{ill|Princess Hashihito|ja|間人皇女}} (consort of {{ill|Emperor Kōtoku|ja|孝徳天皇}}). Excavations in 1977–1978 created measured diagrams based on surveys, and while it was initially reported as a circular tumulus,Ōtsuka, Hatsushige, and Kobayashi, Saburō (1982). *Dictionary of Kofun.* Tokyo: Tōkyodō Publishing, pp. 108-109. the possibility of an octagonal structure was also noted. From September 2009 to September 2010, academic excavations by the Asuka Village Board of Education confirmed the octagonal layout.[http://mainichi.jp/select/wadai/news/20100910k0000m040050000c.html Kengoshizuka Kofun: Confirmed as Octagonal Structure and Likely Burial Site of Empress Saimei.] "Mainichi Shimbun," September 9, 2010.[http://mainichi.jp/select/wadai/news/20100910k0000m040072000c.html Kengoshizuka Kofun: A 550-ton Stone Mausoleum Exhibiting Authority.] "Mainichi Shimbun," September 9, 2010.[http://www.jiji.com/jc/c?g=soc_30&k=2010090900686 Octagonal Mound Confirmed for Kengoshizuka Kofun: Further Evidence of Empress Saimei's Tomb.] "Jiji Press," September 9, 2010. The mound was found to be a triple-tiered octagonal tumulus standing approximately 4.5 meters tall, with the base measuring 22 meters across. Surrounding the mound is a paved stone structure with a similar octagonal shape, extending the total diameter to approximately 32 meters, including gravel layers. Hundreds of meticulously carved white tuff stones were uncovered, estimated to have originally numbered 7,200 and used to create a pyramid-like exterior.Asahi Shimbun, September 10, 2010. == Interior Structure == The interior is a {{ill|yokoguchi-style sekkaku|ja|横口式石槨}} (side-entry stone chamber), partially exposed as of 2009. The chamber is carved from a massive block of tuff weighing approximately 80 tons, sourced from [[:en:Mount_Nijō|Mount Nijō]] 15 kilometers away. The dimensions of the chamber are 5 meters wide, 3.5 meters deep, and 2.5 meters high, divided into two spaces by a central partition wall. The total weight of the stones used in the construction exceeds 550 tons. Transporting such massive stones over long distances required significant manpower, highlighting the power of the centralized state. == Excavated Artifacts == Artifacts include lacquered coffin fragments, gold-copper fittings with {{ill|Cloisonné|ja|七宝}} patterns, glass beads, and human molars believed to belong to Princess Hashihito. These were designated as National Important Cultural Properties in 1953.{{国指定文化財等データベース|201|9725|牽牛子塚古墳出土品}} == Cultural Significance == The Kofun's unique octagonal shape aligns it with other imperial tombs such as the {{ill|Dannotsuka Kofun|ja|段ノ塚古墳}} (tomb of {{ill|Emperor Jomei|ja|舒明天皇}}) and the {{ill|Noguchi Ouka Tomb|ja|野口王墓}} (joint tomb of {{ill|Emperor Tenmu|ja|天武天皇}} and {{ill|Empress Jitō|ja|持統天皇}}). This reinforces its probable identification as the tomb of Empress Saimei. == Adjacent Kofun == In December 2010, the Asuka Village Board of Education announced the discovery of a smaller kofun adjacent to Kengoshizuka Kofun. This nearby tomb, named {{ill|Kosotsukamikado Kofun|ja|越塚御門古墳}}, is hypothesized to be the tomb of Princess Ōta, Empress Saimei's granddaughter.[https://web.archive.org/web/20101211190601/http://www.yomiuri.co.jp/national/culture/news/20101209-OYT1T00770.htm Adjacent Tomb Likely Princess Ōta's Burial Site.] Yomiuri Shimbun, December 9, 2010. == Access == * Approximately 550 meters northwest of {{ill|Asuka Station|ja|飛鳥駅}} ({{ill|Kintetsu Yoshino Line|ja|近鉄吉野線}}). == References == {{Reflist}} == External Links == Mausoleum|mark={{ill|Octagonal Kofun|ja|八角墳}}.svg|marksize=28|caption=|position=bottom|width=200|float=center}} }} '''Kengoshizuka Kofun''' is a [[Kofun]] in [[Asuka, Nara]] Japan.Tokuse, Takahiko, and Eriko Oka. "Life in Archaeological Sites and Settlements in Asuka Village as a Model Case for Managing Settlements Adjacent to Archaeological Sites: A Proposal for the Future of Saqqara." The journal of Center for the Global Study of Cultural Heritage and Culture 2 (2015): 5-20.{{cite book |title=Burial Mounds in Europe and Japan: Comparative and Contextual Perspectives |date=30 September 2018 |doi=10.2307/j.ctv1228gf7|s2cid=240193791 }} Specifically, it is an [[Octagonal Kofun]]. It is said to be the burial site of [[Empress Kōgyoku]].{{Cite web |title=Kengoshizuka Kofun Tumulus, Koshitsuka-gomon Kofun Tumulus |url=http://asuka-japan-heritage.jp/global/en/saimei/detail/kengosiduka_sa.html |access-date=2023-10-20 |website=Exploring the Footsteps of the Heroines of Asuka |language=en}}{{Cite news |date=2022-03-04 |title=Octagonal burial mound said to belong to ancient Japan empress reconstructed in Nara Pref. |language=en |work=Mainichi Daily News |url=https://mainichi.jp/english/articles/20220304/p2a/00m/0na/040000c |access-date=2023-10-20}} it was reconstructed and opened to the public on May 6 2022. This contrasts with other Imperial tombs such as the [[Mausoleum of Emperor Tenji]] which are closed to the public by the [[Imperial Household Agency]].{{Cite web |title=Gobyōyama Kofun (in Kyōto) - Passage Grave in Japan in Honshū |url=https://www.megalithic.co.uk/article.php?sid=33021 |access-date=2023-10-21 |website=The Megalithic Portal}} [[File:220311 Kengoshiduka 3.jpg|thumb|Entrance to the burial chamber]] ==overview== '''Kengoshizuka Kofun''' (牽牛子塚古墳) is a {{ill|Kofun|ja|古墳}} located in {{ill|Asuka, Nara|ja|明日香村}}, {{ill|Nara Prefecture|ja|奈良県}}, Japan. It is an {{ill|Octagonal Kofun|ja|八角墳}} and has been designated as a National Historic Site. The excavated artifacts from the site are designated as National Important Cultural Properties. The name "Kengoshizuka" includes the word "{{ill|Asagao|ja|アサガオ}}" ([[:en:Ipomoea_nil|Morning Glory]]), an alternate reading for "Kengoshi." The tumulus is also referred to as "Omae-zuka."[http://www.asukamura.jp/chosa_hokoku/kengoshizuka/kengoshizuka.html Kengoshizuka Kofun] Asuka Village Official Website Excavations conducted between 2009 and 2010 revealed that the tumulus was octagonal, strengthening its association with {{ill|Empress Saimei|ja|斉明天皇}}, mother of {{ill|Emperor Tenji|ja|天智天皇}} and {{ill|Emperor Tenmu|ja|天武天皇}}. Full restoration was completed in February 2022.Nara's Asuka Morning Glory Kofun fully restored, "Mainichi Shimbun," March 3, 2022, Osaka Morning Edition == location == The tumulus is located near the border of {{ill|Kashihara|ja|橿原市}} and lies at the stable, broad apex of a hill in {{ill|Asuka, Nara|ja|明日香村}}. Its summit reaches an elevation of 126.3 meters and is approximately 500 meters west of the {{ill|Iwayayama Kofun|ja|岩屋山古墳}}, another National Historic Site. == Exterior and Scale == The site was previously known for its unique internal structure, consisting of two hollowed chambers within a massive stone. This led to theories that it served as a combined tomb for Empress Saimei and her daughter {{ill|Princess Hashihito|ja|間人皇女}} (consort of {{ill|Emperor Kōtoku|ja|孝徳天皇}}). Excavations in 1977–1978 created measured diagrams based on surveys, and while it was initially reported as a circular tumulus,Ōtsuka, Hatsushige, and Kobayashi, Saburō (1982). *Dictionary of Kofun.* Tokyo: Tōkyodō Publishing, pp. 108-109. the possibility of an octagonal structure was also noted. From September 2009 to September 2010, academic excavations by the Asuka Village Board of Education confirmed the octagonal layout.[http://mainichi.jp/select/wadai/news/20100910k0000m040050000c.html Kengoshizuka Kofun: Confirmed as Octagonal Structure and Likely Burial Site of Empress Saimei.] "Mainichi Shimbun," September 9, 2010.[http://mainichi.jp/select/wadai/news/20100910k0000m040072000c.html Kengoshizuka Kofun: A 550-ton Stone Mausoleum Exhibiting Authority.] "Mainichi Shimbun," September 9, 2010.[http://www.jiji.com/jc/c?g=soc_30&k=2010090900686 Octagonal Mound Confirmed for Kengoshizuka Kofun: Further Evidence of Empress Saimei's Tomb.] "Jiji Press," September 9, 2010. The mound was found to be a triple-tiered octagonal tumulus standing approximately 4.5 meters tall, with the base measuring 22 meters across. Surrounding the mound is a paved stone structure with a similar octagonal shape, extending the total diameter to approximately 32 meters, including gravel layers. Hundreds of meticulously carved white tuff stones were uncovered, estimated to have originally numbered 7,200 and used to create a pyramid-like exterior.Asahi Shimbun, September 10, 2010. == Interior Structure == The interior is a {{ill|yokoguchi-style sekkaku|ja|横口式石槨}} (side-entry stone chamber), partially exposed as of 2009. The chamber is carved from a massive block of tuff weighing approximately 80 tons, sourced from [[:en:Mount_Nijō|Mount Nijō]] 15 kilometers away. The dimensions of the chamber are 5 meters wide, 3.5 meters deep, and 2.5 meters high, divided into two spaces by a central partition wall. The total weight of the stones used in the construction exceeds 550 tons. Transporting such massive stones over long distances required significant manpower, highlighting the power of the centralized state. == Excavated Artifacts == Artifacts include lacquered coffin fragments, gold-copper fittings with {{ill|Cloisonné|ja|七宝}} patterns, glass beads, and human molars believed to belong to Princess Hashihito. These were designated as National Important Cultural Properties in 1953.{{国指定文化財等データベース|201|9725|牽牛子塚古墳出土品}} == Cultural Significance == The Kofun's unique octagonal shape aligns it with other imperial tombs such as the {{ill|Dannotsuka Kofun|ja|段ノ塚古墳}} (tomb of {{ill|Emperor Jomei|ja|舒明天皇}}) and the {{ill|Noguchi Ouka Tomb|ja|野口王墓}} (joint tomb of {{ill|Emperor Tenmu|ja|天武天皇}} and {{ill|Empress Jitō|ja|持統天皇}}). This reinforces its probable identification as the tomb of Empress Saimei. == Adjacent Kofun == In December 2010, the Asuka Village Board of Education announced the discovery of a smaller kofun adjacent to Kengoshizuka Kofun. This nearby tomb, named {{ill|Kosotsukamikado Kofun|ja|越塚御門古墳}}, is hypothesized to be the tomb of Princess Ōta, Empress Saimei's granddaughter.[https://web.archive.org/web/20101211190601/http://www.yomiuri.co.jp/national/culture/news/20101209-OYT1T00770.htm Adjacent Tomb Likely Princess Ōta's Burial Site.] Yomiuri Shimbun, December 9, 2010. == Access == * Approximately 550 meters northwest of {{ill|Asuka Station|ja|飛鳥駅}} ({{ill|Kintetsu Yoshino Line|ja|近鉄吉野線}}). == References == {{Reflist}} == External Links == Mausoleum|mark={{ill|Octagonal Kofun|ja|八角墳}}.svg|marksize=28|caption=|position=bottom|width=200|float=center}} }} '''Kengoshizuka Kofun''' is a [[Kofun]] in [[Asuka, Nara]] Japan.Tokuse, Takahiko, and Eriko Oka. "Life in Archaeological Sites and Settlements in Asuka Village as a Model Case for Managing Settlements Adjacent to Archaeological Sites: A Proposal for the Future of Saqqara." The journal of Center for the Global Study of Cultural Heritage and Culture 2 (2015): 5-20.{{cite book |title=Burial Mounds in Europe and Japan: Comparative and Contextual Perspectives |date=30 September 2018 |doi=10.2307/j.ctv1228gf7|s2cid=240193791 }} Specifically, it is an [[Octagonal Kofun]]. It is said to be the burial site of [[Empress Kōgyoku]].{{Cite web |title=Kengoshizuka Kofun Tumulus, Koshitsuka-gomon Kofun Tumulus |url=http://asuka-japan-heritage.jp/global/en/saimei/detail/kengosiduka_sa.html |access-date=2023-10-20 |website=Exploring the Footsteps of the Heroines of Asuka |language=en}}{{Cite news |date=2022-03-04 |title=Octagonal burial mound said to belong to ancient Japan empress reconstructed in Nara Pref. |language=en |work=Mainichi Daily News |url=https://mainichi.jp/english/articles/20220304/p2a/00m/0na/040000c |access-date=2023-10-20}} it was reconstructed and opened to the public on May 6 2022. This contrasts with other Imperial tombs such as the [[Mausoleum of Emperor Tenji]] which are closed to the public by the [[Imperial Household Agency]].{{Cite web |title=Gobyōyama Kofun (in Kyōto) - Passage Grave in Japan in Honshū |url=https://www.megalithic.co.uk/article.php?sid=33021 |access-date=2023-10-21 |website=The Megalithic Portal}} [[File:220311 Kengoshiduka 3.jpg|thumb|Entrance to the burial chamber]] ==overview== '''Kengoshizuka Kofun''' (牽牛子塚古墳) is a {{ill|Kofun|ja|古墳}} located in {{ill|Asuka, Nara|ja|明日香村}}, {{ill|Nara Prefecture|ja|奈良県}}, Japan. It is an {{ill|Octagonal Kofun|ja|八角墳}} and has been designated as a National Historic Site. The excavated artifacts from the site are designated as National Important Cultural Properties. The name "Kengoshizuka" includes the word "{{ill|Asagao|ja|アサガオ}}" ([[:en:Ipomoea_nil|Morning Glory]]), an alternate reading for "Kengoshi." The tumulus is also referred to as "Omae-zuka."[http://www.asukamura.jp/chosa_hokoku/kengoshizuka/kengoshizuka.html Kengoshizuka Kofun] Asuka Village Official Website Excavations conducted between 2009 and 2010 revealed that the tumulus was octagonal, strengthening its association with {{ill|Empress Saimei|ja|斉明天皇}}, mother of {{ill|Emperor Tenji|ja|天智天皇}} and {{ill|Emperor Tenmu|ja|天武天皇}}. Full restoration was completed in February 2022.Nara's Asuka Morning Glory Kofun fully restored, "Mainichi Shimbun," March 3, 2022, Osaka Morning Edition == location == The tumulus is located near the border of {{ill|Kashihara|ja|橿原市}} and lies at the stable, broad apex of a hill in {{ill|Asuka, Nara|ja|明日香村}}. Its summit reaches an elevation of 126.3 meters and is approximately 500 meters west of the {{ill|Iwayayama Kofun|ja|岩屋山古墳}}, another National Historic Site. == Exterior and Scale == The site was previously known for its unique internal structure, consisting of two hollowed chambers within a massive stone. This led to theories that it served as a combined tomb for Empress Saimei and her daughter {{ill|Princess Hashihito|ja|間人皇女}} (consort of {{ill|Emperor Kōtoku|ja|孝徳天皇}}). Excavations in 1977–1978 created measured diagrams based on surveys, and while it was initially reported as a circular tumulus,Ōtsuka, Hatsushige, and Kobayashi, Saburō (1982). *Dictionary of Kofun.* Tokyo: Tōkyodō Publishing, pp. 108-109. the possibility of an octagonal structure was also noted. From September 2009 to September 2010, academic excavations by the Asuka Village Board of Education confirmed the octagonal layout.[http://mainichi.jp/select/wadai/news/20100910k0000m040050000c.html Kengoshizuka Kofun: Confirmed as Octagonal Structure and Likely Burial Site of Empress Saimei.] "Mainichi Shimbun," September 9, 2010.[http://mainichi.jp/select/wadai/news/20100910k0000m040072000c.html Kengoshizuka Kofun: A 550-ton Stone Mausoleum Exhibiting Authority.] "Mainichi Shimbun," September 9, 2010.[http://www.jiji.com/jc/c?g=soc_30&k=2010090900686 Octagonal Mound Confirmed for Kengoshizuka Kofun: Further Evidence of Empress Saimei's Tomb.] "Jiji Press," September 9, 2010. The mound was found to be a triple-tiered octagonal tumulus standing approximately 4.5 meters tall, with the base measuring 22 meters across. Surrounding the mound is a paved stone structure with a similar octagonal shape, extending the total diameter to approximately 32 meters, including gravel layers. Hundreds of meticulously carved white tuff stones were uncovered, estimated to have originally numbered 7,200 and used to create a pyramid-like exterior.Asahi Shimbun, September 10, 2010. == Interior Structure == The interior is a {{ill|yokoguchi-style sekkaku|ja|横口式石槨}} (side-entry stone chamber), partially exposed as of 2009. The chamber is carved from a massive block of tuff weighing approximately 80 tons, sourced from [[:en:Mount_Nijō|Mount Nijō]] 15 kilometers away. The dimensions of the chamber are 5 meters wide, 3.5 meters deep, and 2.5 meters high, divided into two spaces by a central partition wall. The total weight of the stones used in the construction exceeds 550 tons. Transporting such massive stones over long distances required significant manpower, highlighting the power of the centralized state. == Excavated Artifacts == Artifacts include lacquered coffin fragments, gold-copper fittings with {{ill|Cloisonné|ja|七宝}} patterns, glass beads, and human molars believed to belong to Princess Hashihito. These were designated as National Important Cultural Properties in 1953.{{国指定文化財等データベース|201|9725|牽牛子塚古墳出土品}} == Cultural Significance == The Kofun's unique octagonal shape aligns it with other imperial tombs such as the {{ill|Dannotsuka Kofun|ja|段ノ塚古墳}} (tomb of {{ill|Emperor Jomei|ja|舒明天皇}}) and the {{ill|Noguchi Ouka Tomb|ja|野口王墓}} (joint tomb of {{ill|Emperor Tenmu|ja|天武天皇}} and {{ill|Empress Jitō|ja|持統天皇}}). This reinforces its probable identification as the tomb of Empress Saimei. == Adjacent Kofun == In December 2010, the Asuka Village Board of Education announced the discovery of a smaller kofun adjacent to Kengoshizuka Kofun. This nearby tomb, named {{ill|Kosotsukamikado Kofun|ja|越塚御門古墳}}, is hypothesized to be the tomb of Princess Ōta, Empress Saimei's granddaughter.[https://web.archive.org/web/20101211190601/http://www.yomiuri.co.jp/national/culture/news/20101209-OYT1T00770.htm Adjacent Tomb Likely Princess Ōta's Burial Site.] Yomiuri Shimbun, December 9, 2010. == Access == * Approximately 550 meters northwest of {{ill|Asuka Station|ja|飛鳥駅}} ({{ill|Kintetsu Yoshino Line|ja|近鉄吉野線}}). == References == {{Reflist}} == External Links == Mausoleum|mark={{ill|Octagonal Kofun|ja|八角墳}}.svg|marksize=28|caption=|position=bottom|width=200|float=center}} }} '''Kengoshizuka Kofun''' is a [[Kofun]] in [[Asuka, Nara]] Japan.Tokuse, Takahiko, and Eriko Oka. "Life in Archaeological Sites and Settlements in Asuka Village as a Model Case for Managing Settlements Adjacent to Archaeological Sites: A Proposal for the Future of Saqqara." The journal of Center for the Global Study of Cultural Heritage and Culture 2 (2015): 5-20.{{cite book |title=Burial Mounds in Europe and Japan: Comparative and Contextual Perspectives |date=30 September 2018 |doi=10.2307/j.ctv1228gf7|s2cid=240193791 }} Specifically, it is an [[Octagonal Kofun]]. It is said to be the burial site of [[Empress Kōgyoku]].{{Cite web |title=Kengoshizuka Kofun Tumulus, Koshitsuka-gomon Kofun Tumulus |url=http://asuka-japan-heritage.jp/global/en/saimei/detail/kengosiduka_sa.html |access-date=2023-10-20 |website=Exploring the Footsteps of the Heroines of Asuka |language=en}}{{Cite news |date=2022-03-04 |title=Octagonal burial mound said to belong to ancient Japan empress reconstructed in Nara Pref. |language=en |work=Mainichi Daily News |url=https://mainichi.jp/english/articles/20220304/p2a/00m/0na/040000c |access-date=2023-10-20}} it was reconstructed and opened to the public on May 6 2022. This contrasts with other Imperial tombs such as the [[Mausoleum of Emperor Tenji]] which are closed to the public by the [[Imperial Household Agency]].{{Cite web |title=Gobyōyama Kofun (in Kyōto) - Passage Grave in Japan in Honshū |url=https://www.megalithic.co.uk/article.php?sid=33021 |access-date=2023-10-21 |website=The Megalithic Portal}} [[File:220311 Kengoshiduka 3.jpg|thumb|Entrance to the burial chamber]] ==overview== '''Kengoshizuka Kofun''' (牽牛子塚古墳) is a {{ill|Kofun|ja|古墳}} located in {{ill|Asuka, Nara|ja|明日香村}}, {{ill|Nara Prefecture|ja|奈良県}}, Japan. It is an {{ill|Octagonal Kofun|ja|八角墳}} and has been designated as a National Historic Site. The excavated artifacts from the site are designated as National Important Cultural Properties. The name "Kengoshizuka" includes the word "{{ill|Asagao|ja|アサガオ}}" ([[:en:Ipomoea_nil|Morning Glory]]), an alternate reading for "Kengoshi." The tumulus is also referred to as "Omae-zuka."[http://www.asukamura.jp/chosa_hokoku/kengoshizuka/kengoshizuka.html Kengoshizuka Kofun] Asuka Village Official Website Excavations conducted between 2009 and 2010 revealed that the tumulus was octagonal, strengthening its association with {{ill|Empress Saimei|ja|斉明天皇}}, mother of {{ill|Emperor Tenji|ja|天智天皇}} and {{ill|Emperor Tenmu|ja|天武天皇}}. Full restoration was completed in February 2022.Nara's Asuka Morning Glory Kofun fully restored, "Mainichi Shimbun," March 3, 2022, Osaka Morning Edition == location == The tumulus is located near the border of {{ill|Kashihara|ja|橿原市}} and lies at the stable, broad apex of a hill in {{ill|Asuka, Nara|ja|明日香村}}. Its summit reaches an elevation of 126.3 meters and is approximately 500 meters west of the {{ill|Iwayayama Kofun|ja|岩屋山古墳}}, another National Historic Site. == Exterior and Scale == The site was previously known for its unique internal structure, consisting of two hollowed chambers within a massive stone. This led to theories that it served as a combined tomb for Empress Saimei and her daughter {{ill|Princess Hashihito|ja|間人皇女}} (consort of {{ill|Emperor Kōtoku|ja|孝徳天皇}}). Excavations in 1977–1978 created measured diagrams based on surveys, and while it was initially reported as a circular tumulus,Ōtsuka, Hatsushige, and Kobayashi, Saburō (1982). *Dictionary of Kofun.* Tokyo: Tōkyodō Publishing, pp. 108-109. the possibility of an octagonal structure was also noted. From September 2009 to September 2010, academic excavations by the Asuka Village Board of Education confirmed the octagonal layout.[http://mainichi.jp/select/wadai/news/20100910k0000m040050000c.html Kengoshizuka Kofun: Confirmed as Octagonal Structure and Likely Burial Site of Empress Saimei.] "Mainichi Shimbun," September 9, 2010.[http://mainichi.jp/select/wadai/news/20100910k0000m040072000c.html Kengoshizuka Kofun: A 550-ton Stone Mausoleum Exhibiting Authority.] "Mainichi Shimbun," September 9, 2010.[http://www.jiji.com/jc/c?g=soc_30&k=2010090900686 Octagonal Mound Confirmed for Kengoshizuka Kofun: Further Evidence of Empress Saimei's Tomb.] "Jiji Press," September 9, 2010. The mound was found to be a triple-tiered octagonal tumulus standing approximately 4.5 meters tall, with the base measuring 22 meters across. Surrounding the mound is a paved stone structure with a similar octagonal shape, extending the total diameter to approximately 32 meters, including gravel layers. Hundreds of meticulously carved white tuff stones were uncovered, estimated to have originally numbered 7,200 and used to create a pyramid-like exterior.Asahi Shimbun, September 10, 2010. == Interior Structure == The interior is a {{ill|yokoguchi-style sekkaku|ja|横口式石槨}} (side-entry stone chamber), partially exposed as of 2009. The chamber is carved from a massive block of tuff weighing approximately 80 tons, sourced from [[:en:Mount_Nijō|Mount Nijō]] 15 kilometers away. The dimensions of the chamber are 5 meters wide, 3.5 meters deep, and 2.5 meters high, divided into two spaces by a central partition wall. The total weight of the stones used in the construction exceeds 550 tons. Transporting such massive stones over long distances required significant manpower, highlighting the power of the centralized state. == Excavated Artifacts == Artifacts include lacquered coffin fragments, gold-copper fittings with {{ill|Cloisonné|ja|七宝}} patterns, glass beads, and human molars believed to belong to Princess Hashihito. These were designated as National Important Cultural Properties in 1953.{{国指定文化財等データベース|201|9725|牽牛子塚古墳出土品}} == Cultural Significance == The Kofun's unique octagonal shape aligns it with other imperial tombs such as the {{ill|Dannotsuka Kofun|ja|段ノ塚古墳}} (tomb of {{ill|Emperor Jomei|ja|舒明天皇}}) and the {{ill|Noguchi Ouka Tomb|ja|野口王墓}} (joint tomb of {{ill|Emperor Tenmu|ja|天武天皇}} and {{ill|Empress Jitō|ja|持統天皇}}). This reinforces its probable identification as the tomb of Empress Saimei. == Adjacent Kofun == In December 2010, the Asuka Village Board of Education announced the discovery of a smaller kofun adjacent to Kengoshizuka Kofun. This nearby tomb, named {{ill|Kosotsukamikado Kofun|ja|越塚御門古墳}}, is hypothesized to be the tomb of Princess Ōta, Empress Saimei's granddaughter.[https://web.archive.org/web/20101211190601/http://www.yomiuri.co.jp/national/culture/news/20101209-OYT1T00770.htm Adjacent Tomb Likely Princess Ōta's Burial Site.] Yomiuri Shimbun, December 9, 2010. == Access == * Approximately 550 meters northwest of {{ill|Asuka Station|ja|飛鳥駅}} ({{ill|Kintetsu Yoshino Line|ja|近鉄吉野線}}). == References == {{Reflist}} == External Links == It is an {{ill|Octagonal Kofun|ja|八角墳}} and has been designated as a National Historic Site. The excavated artifacts from the site are designated as National Important Cultural Properties. The name "Kengoshizuka" includes the word "{{ill|Asagao|ja|アサガオ}}" ([[:en:Ipomoea_nil|Morning Glory]]), an alternate reading for "Kengoshi." The tumulus is also referred to as "Omae-zuka."[http://www.asukamura.jp/chosa_hokoku/kengoshizuka/kengoshizuka.html Kengoshizuka Kofun] Asuka Village Official Website Excavations conducted between 2009 and 2010 revealed that the tumulus was octagonal, strengthening its association with {{ill|Empress Saimei|ja|斉明天皇}}, mother of {{ill|Emperor Tenji|ja|天智天皇}} and {{ill|Emperor Tenmu|ja|天武天皇}}. Full restoration was completed in February 2022.Nara's Asuka Morning Glory Kofun fully restored, "Mainichi Shimbun," March 3, 2022, Osaka Morning Edition == location == The tumulus is located near the border of {{ill|Kashihara|ja|橿原市}} and lies at the stable, broad apex of a hill in {{ill|Asuka, Nara|ja|明日香村}}. Its summit reaches an elevation of 126.3 meters and is approximately 500 meters west of the {{ill|Iwayayama Kofun|ja|岩屋山古墳}}, another National Historic Site. == Exterior and Scale == The site was previously known for its unique internal structure, consisting of two hollowed chambers within a massive stone. This led to theories that it served as a combined tomb for Empress Saimei and her daughter {{ill|Princess Hashihito|ja|間人皇女}} (consort of {{ill|Emperor Kōtoku|ja|孝徳天皇}}). Excavations in 1977–1978 created measured diagrams based on surveys, and while it was initially reported as a circular tumulus,Ōtsuka, Hatsushige, and Kobayashi, Saburō (1982). *Dictionary of Kofun.* Tokyo: Tōkyodō Publishing, pp. 108-109. the possibility of an octagonal structure was also noted. From September 2009 to September 2010, academic excavations by the Asuka Village Board of Education confirmed the octagonal layout.[http://mainichi.jp/select/wadai/news/20100910k0000m040050000c.html Kengoshizuka Kofun: Confirmed as Octagonal Structure and Likely Burial Site of Empress Saimei.] "Mainichi Shimbun," September 9, 2010.[http://mainichi.jp/select/wadai/news/20100910k0000m040072000c.html Kengoshizuka Kofun: A 550-ton Stone Mausoleum Exhibiting Authority.] "Mainichi Shimbun," September 9, 2010.[http://www.jiji.com/jc/c?g=soc_30&k=2010090900686 Octagonal Mound Confirmed for Kengoshizuka Kofun: Further Evidence of Empress Saimei's Tomb.] "Jiji Press," September 9, 2010. The mound was found to be a triple-tiered octagonal tumulus standing approximately 4.5 meters tall, with the base measuring 22 meters across. Surrounding the mound is a paved stone structure with a similar octagonal shape, extending the total diameter to approximately 32 meters, including gravel layers. Hundreds of meticulously carved white tuff stones were uncovered, estimated to have originally numbered 7,200 and used to create a pyramid-like exterior.Asahi Shimbun, September 10, 2010. == Interior Structure == The interior is a {{ill|yokoguchi-style sekkaku|ja|横口式石槨}} (side-entry stone chamber), partially exposed as of 2009. The chamber is carved from a massive block of tuff weighing approximately 80 tons, sourced from [[:en:Mount_Nijō|Mount Nijō]] 15 kilometers away. The dimensions of the chamber are 5 meters wide, 3.5 meters deep, and 2.5 meters high, divided into two spaces by a central partition wall. The total weight of the stones used in the construction exceeds 550 tons. Transporting such massive stones over long distances required significant manpower, highlighting the power of the centralized state. == Excavated Artifacts == Artifacts include lacquered coffin fragments, gold-copper fittings with {{ill|Cloisonné|ja|七宝}} patterns, glass beads, and human molars believed to belong to Princess Hashihito. These were designated as National Important Cultural Properties in 1953.{{国指定文化財等データベース|201|9725|牽牛子塚古墳出土品}} == Cultural Significance == The Kofun's unique octagonal shape aligns it with other imperial tombs such as the {{ill|Dannotsuka Kofun|ja|段ノ塚古墳}} (tomb of {{ill|Emperor Jomei|ja|舒明天皇}}) and the {{ill|Noguchi Ouka Tomb|ja|野口王墓}} (joint tomb of {{ill|Emperor Tenmu|ja|天武天皇}} and {{ill|Empress Jitō|ja|持統天皇}}). This reinforces its probable identification as the tomb of Empress Saimei. == Adjacent Kofun == In December 2010, the Asuka Village Board of Education announced the discovery of a smaller kofun adjacent to Kengoshizuka Kofun. This nearby tomb, named {{ill|Kosotsukamikado Kofun|ja|越塚御門古墳}}, is hypothesized to be the tomb of Princess Ōta, Empress Saimei's granddaughter.[https://web.archive.org/web/20101211190601/http://www.yomiuri.co.jp/national/culture/news/20101209-OYT1T00770.htm Adjacent Tomb Likely Princess Ōta's Burial Site.] Yomiuri Shimbun, December 9, 2010. == Access == * Approximately 550 meters northwest of {{ill|Asuka Station|ja|飛鳥駅}} ({{ill|Kintetsu Yoshino Line|ja|近鉄吉野線}}). == References == {{Reflist}} == External Links == Hundreds of meticulously carved white tuff stones were uncovered, estimated to have originally numbered 7,200 and used to create a pyramid-like exterior.Asahi Shimbun, September 10, 2010. == Interior Structure == The interior is a {{ill|yokoguchi-style sekkaku|ja|横口式石槨}} (side-entry stone chamber), partially exposed as of 2009. The chamber is carved from a massive block of tuff weighing approximately 80 tons, sourced from [[:en:Mount_Nijō|Mount Nijō]] 15 kilometers away. The dimensions of the chamber are 5 meters wide, 3.5 meters deep, and 2.5 meters high, divided into two spaces by a central partition wall. The total weight of the stones used in the construction exceeds 550 tons. Transporting such massive stones over long distances required significant manpower, highlighting the power of the centralized state. == Excavated Artifacts == Artifacts include lacquered coffin fragments, gold-copper fittings with {{ill|Cloisonné|ja|七宝}} patterns, glass beads, and human molars believed to belong to Princess Hashihito. These were designated as National Important Cultural Properties in 1953.{{国指定文化財等データベース|201|9725|牽牛子塚古墳出土品}} == Cultural Significance == The Kofun's unique octagonal shape aligns it with other imperial tombs such as the {{ill|Dannotsuka Kofun|ja|段ノ塚古墳}} (tomb of {{ill|Emperor Jomei|ja|舒明天皇}}) and the {{ill|Noguchi Ouka Tomb|ja|野口王墓}} (joint tomb of {{ill|Emperor Tenmu|ja|天武天皇}} and {{ill|Empress Jitō|ja|持統天皇}}). This reinforces its probable identification as the tomb of Empress Saimei. == Adjacent Kofun == In December 2010, the Asuka Village Board of Education announced the discovery of a smaller kofun adjacent to Kengoshizuka Kofun. This nearby tomb, named {{ill|Kosotsukamikado Kofun|ja|越塚御門古墳}}, is hypothesized to be the tomb of Princess Ōta, Empress Saimei's granddaughter.[https://web.archive.org/web/20101211190601/http://www.yomiuri.co.jp/national/culture/news/20101209-OYT1T00770.htm Adjacent Tomb Likely Princess Ōta's Burial Site.] Yomiuri Shimbun, December 9, 2010. == Access == * Approximately 550 meters northwest of {{ill|Asuka Station|ja|飛鳥駅}} ({{ill|Kintetsu Yoshino Line|ja|近鉄吉野線}}). == References == {{Reflist}} == External Links == Mausoleum|mark={{ill|Octagonal Kofun|ja|八角墳}}.svg|marksize=28|caption=|position=bottom|width=200|float=center}} }} '''Kengoshizuka Kofun''' is a [[Kofun]] in [[Asuka, Nara]] Japan.Tokuse, Takahiko, and Eriko Oka. "Life in Archaeological Sites and Settlements in Asuka Village as a Model Case for Managing Settlements Adjacent to Archaeological Sites: A Proposal for the Future of Saqqara." The journal of Center for the Global Study of Cultural Heritage and Culture 2 (2015): 5-20.{{cite book |title=Burial Mounds in Europe and Japan: Comparative and Contextual Perspectives |date=30 September 2018 |doi=10.2307/j.ctv1228gf7|s2cid=240193791 }} Specifically, it is an [[Octagonal Kofun]]. It is said to be the burial site of [[Empress Kōgyoku]].{{Cite web |title=Kengoshizuka Kofun Tumulus, Koshitsuka-gomon Kofun Tumulus |url=http://asuka-japan-heritage.jp/global/en/saimei/detail/kengosiduka_sa.html |access-date=2023-10-20 |website=Exploring the Footsteps of the Heroines of Asuka |language=en}}{{Cite news |date=2022-03-04 |title=Octagonal burial mound said to belong to ancient Japan empress reconstructed in Nara Pref. |language=en |work=Mainichi Daily News |url=https://mainichi.jp/english/articles/20220304/p2a/00m/0na/040000c |access-date=2023-10-20}} it was reconstructed and opened to the public on May 6 2022. This contrasts with other Imperial tombs such as the [[Mausoleum of Emperor Tenji]] which are closed to the public by the [[Imperial Household Agency]].{{Cite web |title=Gobyōyama Kofun (in Kyōto) - Passage Grave in Japan in Honshū |url=https://www.megalithic.co.uk/article.php?sid=33021 |access-date=2023-10-21 |website=The Megalithic Portal}} [[File:220311 Kengoshiduka 3.jpg|thumb|Entrance to the burial chamber]] ==overview== '''Kengoshizuka Kofun''' (牽牛子塚古墳) is a {{ill|Kofun|ja|古墳}} located in {{ill|Asuka, Nara|ja|明日香村}}, {{ill|Nara Prefecture|ja|奈良県}}, Japan. It is an {{ill|Octagonal Kofun|ja|八角墳}} and has been designated as a National Historic Site. The excavated artifacts from the site are designated as National Important Cultural Properties. The name "Kengoshizuka" includes the word "{{ill|Asagao|ja|アサガオ}}" ([[:en:Ipomoea_nil|Morning Glory]]), an alternate reading for "Kengoshi." The tumulus is also referred to as "Omae-zuka."[http://www.asukamura.jp/chosa_hokoku/kengoshizuka/kengoshizuka.html Kengoshizuka Kofun] Asuka Village Official Website Excavations conducted between 2009 and 2010 revealed that the tumulus was octagonal, strengthening its association with {{ill|Empress Saimei|ja|斉明天皇}}, mother of {{ill|Emperor Tenji|ja|天智天皇}} and {{ill|Emperor Tenmu|ja|天武天皇}}. Full restoration was completed in February 2022.Nara's Asuka Morning Glory Kofun fully restored, "Mainichi Shimbun," March 3, 2022, Osaka Morning Edition == location == The tumulus is located near the border of {{ill|Kashihara|ja|橿原市}} and lies at the stable, broad apex of a hill in {{ill|Asuka, Nara|ja|明日香村}}. Its summit reaches an elevation of 126.3 meters and is approximately 500 meters west of the {{ill|Iwayayama Kofun|ja|岩屋山古墳}}, another National Historic Site. == Exterior and Scale == The site was previously known for its unique internal structure, consisting of two hollowed chambers within a massive stone. This led to theories that it served as a combined tomb for Empress Saimei and her daughter {{ill|Princess Hashihito|ja|間人皇女}} (consort of {{ill|Emperor Kōtoku|ja|孝徳天皇}}). Excavations in 1977–1978 created measured diagrams based on surveys, and while it was initially reported as a circular tumulus,Ōtsuka, Hatsushige, and Kobayashi, Saburō (1982). *Dictionary of Kofun.* Tokyo: Tōkyodō Publishing, pp. 108-109. the possibility of an octagonal structure was also noted. From September 2009 to September 2010, academic excavations by the Asuka Village Board of Education confirmed the octagonal layout.[http://mainichi.jp/select/wadai/news/20100910k0000m040050000c.html Kengoshizuka Kofun: Confirmed as Octagonal Structure and Likely Burial Site of Empress Saimei.] "Mainichi Shimbun," September 9, 2010.[http://mainichi.jp/select/wadai/news/20100910k0000m040072000c.html Kengoshizuka Kofun: A 550-ton Stone Mausoleum Exhibiting Authority.] "Mainichi Shimbun," September 9, 2010.[http://www.jiji.com/jc/c?g=soc_30&k=2010090900686 Octagonal Mound Confirmed for Kengoshizuka Kofun: Further Evidence of Empress Saimei's Tomb.] "Jiji Press," September 9, 2010. The mound was found to be a triple-tiered octagonal tumulus standing approximately 4.5 meters tall, with the base measuring 22 meters across. Surrounding the mound is a paved stone structure with a similar octagonal shape, extending the total diameter to approximately 32 meters, including gravel layers. Hundreds of meticulously carved white tuff stones were uncovered, estimated to have originally numbered 7,200 and used to create a pyramid-like exterior.Asahi Shimbun, September 10, 2010. == Interior Structure == The interior is a {{ill|yokoguchi-style sekkaku|ja|横口式石槨}} (side-entry stone chamber), partially exposed as of 2009. The chamber is carved from a massive block of tuff weighing approximately 80 tons, sourced from [[:en:Mount_Nijō|Mount Nijō]] 15 kilometers away. The dimensions of the chamber are 5 meters wide, 3.5 meters deep, and 2.5 meters high, divided into two spaces by a central partition wall. The total weight of the stones used in the construction exceeds 550 tons. Transporting such massive stones over long distances required significant manpower, highlighting the power of the centralized state. == Excavated Artifacts == Artifacts include lacquered coffin fragments, gold-copper fittings with {{ill|Cloisonné|ja|七宝}} patterns, glass beads, and human molars believed to belong to Princess Hashihito. These were designated as National Important Cultural Properties in 1953.{{国指定文化財等データベース|201|9725|牽牛子塚古墳出土品}} == Cultural Significance == The Kofun's unique octagonal shape aligns it with other imperial tombs such as the {{ill|Dannotsuka Kofun|ja|段ノ塚古墳}} (tomb of {{ill|Emperor Jomei|ja|舒明天皇}}) and the {{ill|Noguchi Ouka Tomb|ja|野口王墓}} (joint tomb of {{ill|Emperor Tenmu|ja|天武天皇}} and {{ill|Empress Jitō|ja|持統天皇}}). This reinforces its probable identification as the tomb of Empress Saimei. == Adjacent Kofun == In December 2010, the Asuka Village Board of Education announced the discovery of a smaller kofun adjacent to Kengoshizuka Kofun. This nearby tomb, named {{ill|Kosotsukamikado Kofun|ja|越塚御門古墳}}, is hypothesized to be the tomb of Princess Ōta, Empress Saimei's granddaughter.[https://web.archive.org/web/20101211190601/http://www.yomiuri.co.jp/national/culture/news/20101209-OYT1T00770.htm Adjacent Tomb Likely Princess Ōta's Burial Site.] Yomiuri Shimbun, December 9, 2010. == Access == * Approximately 550 meters northwest of {{ill|Asuka Station|ja|飛鳥駅}} ({{ill|Kintetsu Yoshino Line|ja|近鉄吉野線}}). == References == {{Reflist}} == External Links == Mausoleum|mark={{ill|Octagonal Kofun|ja|八角墳}}.svg|marksize=28|caption=|position=bottom|width=200|float=center}} }} '''Kengoshizuka Kofun''' is a [[Kofun]] in [[Asuka, Nara]] Japan.Tokuse, Takahiko, and Eriko Oka. "Life in Archaeological Sites and Settlements in Asuka Village as a Model Case for Managing Settlements Adjacent to Archaeological Sites: A Proposal for the Future of Saqqara." The journal of Center for the Global Study of Cultural Heritage and Culture 2 (2015): 5-20.{{cite book |title=Burial Mounds in Europe and Japan: Comparative and Contextual Perspectives |date=30 September 2018 |doi=10.2307/j.ctv1228gf7|s2cid=240193791 }} Specifically, it is an [[Octagonal Kofun]]. It is said to be the burial site of [[Empress Kōgyoku]].{{Cite web |title=Kengoshizuka Kofun Tumulus, Koshitsuka-gomon Kofun Tumulus |url=http://asuka-japan-heritage.jp/global/en/saimei/detail/kengosiduka_sa.html |access-date=2023-10-20 |website=Exploring the Footsteps of the Heroines of Asuka |language=en}}{{Cite news |date=2022-03-04 |title=Octagonal burial mound said to belong to ancient Japan empress reconstructed in Nara Pref. |language=en |work=Mainichi Daily News |url=https://mainichi.jp/english/articles/20220304/p2a/00m/0na/040000c |access-date=2023-10-20}} it was reconstructed and opened to the public on May 6 2022. This contrasts with other Imperial tombs such as the [[Mausoleum of Emperor Tenji]] which are closed to the public by the [[Imperial Household Agency]].{{Cite web |title=Gobyōyama Kofun (in Kyōto) - Passage Grave in Japan in Honshū |url=https://www.megalithic.co.uk/article.php?sid=33021 |access-date=2023-10-21 |website=The Megalithic Portal}} [[File:220311 Kengoshiduka 3.jpg|thumb|Entrance to the burial chamber]] ==overview== '''Kengoshizuka Kofun''' (牽牛子塚古墳) is a {{ill|Kofun|ja|古墳}} located in {{ill|Asuka, Nara|ja|明日香村}}, {{ill|Nara Prefecture|ja|奈良県}}, Japan. It is an {{ill|Octagonal Kofun|ja|八角墳}} and has been designated as a National Historic Site. The excavated artifacts from the site are designated as National Important Cultural Properties. The name "Kengoshizuka" includes the word "{{ill|Asagao|ja|アサガオ}}" ([[:en:Ipomoea_nil|Morning Glory]]), an alternate reading for "Kengoshi." The tumulus is also referred to as "Omae-zuka."[http://www.asukamura.jp/chosa_hokoku/kengoshizuka/kengoshizuka.html Kengoshizuka Kofun] Asuka Village Official Website Excavations conducted between 2009 and 2010 revealed that the tumulus was octagonal, strengthening its association with {{ill|Empress Saimei|ja|斉明天皇}}, mother of {{ill|Emperor Tenji|ja|天智天皇}} and {{ill|Emperor Tenmu|ja|天武天皇}}. Full restoration was completed in February 2022.Nara's Asuka Morning Glory Kofun fully restored, "Mainichi Shimbun," March 3, 2022, Osaka Morning Edition == location == The tumulus is located near the border of {{ill|Kashihara|ja|橿原市}} and lies at the stable, broad apex of a hill in {{ill|Asuka, Nara|ja|明日香村}}. Its summit reaches an elevation of 126.3 meters and is approximately 500 meters west of the {{ill|Iwayayama Kofun|ja|岩屋山古墳}}, another National Historic Site. == Exterior and Scale == The site was previously known for its unique internal structure, consisting of two hollowed chambers within a massive stone. This led to theories that it served as a combined tomb for Empress Saimei and her daughter {{ill|Princess Hashihito|ja|間人皇女}} (consort of {{ill|Emperor Kōtoku|ja|孝徳天皇}}). Excavations in 1977–1978 created measured diagrams based on surveys, and while it was initially reported as a circular tumulus,Ōtsuka, Hatsushige, and Kobayashi, Saburō (1982). *Dictionary of Kofun.* Tokyo: Tōkyodō Publishing, pp. 108-109. the possibility of an octagonal structure was also noted. From September 2009 to September 2010, academic excavations by the Asuka Village Board of Education confirmed the octagonal layout.[http://mainichi.jp/select/wadai/news/20100910k0000m040050000c.html Kengoshizuka Kofun: Confirmed as Octagonal Structure and Likely Burial Site of Empress Saimei.] "Mainichi Shimbun," September 9, 2010.[http://mainichi.jp/select/wadai/news/20100910k0000m040072000c.html Kengoshizuka Kofun: A 550-ton Stone Mausoleum Exhibiting Authority.] "Mainichi Shimbun," September 9, 2010.[http://www.jiji.com/jc/c?g=soc_30&k=2010090900686 Octagonal Mound Confirmed for Kengoshizuka Kofun: Further Evidence of Empress Saimei's Tomb.] "Jiji Press," September 9, 2010. The mound was found to be a triple-tiered octagonal tumulus standing approximately 4.5 meters tall, with the base measuring 22 meters across. Surrounding the mound is a paved stone structure with a similar octagonal shape, extending the total diameter to approximately 32 meters, including gravel layers. Hundreds of meticulously carved white tuff stones were uncovered, estimated to have originally numbered 7,200 and used to create a pyramid-like exterior.Asahi Shimbun, September 10, 2010. == Interior Structure == The interior is a {{ill|yokoguchi-style sekkaku|ja|横口式石槨|1=Side-entrance Sarcophagus Chamber}} (side-entry stone chamber), partially exposed as of 2009. The chamber is carved from a massive block of tuff weighing approximately 80 tons, sourced from [[:en:Mount_Nijō|Mount Nijō]] 15 kilometers away. The dimensions of the chamber are 5 meters wide, 3.5 meters deep, and 2.5 meters high, divided into two spaces by a central partition wall. The total weight of the stones used in the construction exceeds 550 tons. Transporting such massive stones over long distances required significant manpower, highlighting the power of the centralized state. == Excavated Artifacts == Artifacts include lacquered coffin fragments, gold-copper fittings with {{ill|Cloisonné|ja|七宝}} patterns, glass beads, and human molars believed to belong to Princess Hashihito. These were designated as National Important Cultural Properties in 1953.{{国指定文化財等データベース|201|9725|牽牛子塚古墳出土品}} == Cultural Significance == The Kofun's unique octagonal shape aligns it with other imperial tombs such as the {{ill|Dannotsuka Kofun|ja|段ノ塚古墳}} (tomb of {{ill|Emperor Jomei|ja|舒明天皇}}) and the {{ill|Noguchi Ouka Tomb|ja|野口王墓}} (joint tomb of {{ill|Emperor Tenmu|ja|天武天皇}} and {{ill|Empress Jitō|ja|持統天皇}}). This reinforces its probable identification as the tomb of Empress Saimei. == Adjacent Kofun == In December 2010, the Asuka Village Board of Education announced the discovery of a smaller kofun adjacent to Kengoshizuka Kofun. This nearby tomb, named {{ill|Kosotsukamikado Kofun|ja|越塚御門古墳}}, is hypothesized to be the tomb of Princess Ōta, Empress Saimei's granddaughter.[https://web.archive.org/web/20101211190601/http://www.yomiuri.co.jp/national/culture/news/20101209-OYT1T00770.htm Adjacent Tomb Likely Princess Ōta's Burial Site.] Yomiuri Shimbun, December 9, 2010. == Access == * Approximately 550 meters northwest of {{ill|Asuka Station|ja|飛鳥駅}} ({{ill|Kintetsu Yoshino Line|ja|近鉄吉野線}}). == References == {{Reflist}} == External Links == {{afc comment|1=idk what to do with this because the wikipedia page was expanded heavily in a different direction on enwiki[[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 03:21, 14 February 2025 (UTC)}} {{Short description|Tomb of Empress Kōgyoku of Japan}}{{Expand Japanese}}{{Infobox ancient site |name=Kengoshizuka Kofun |image=[[File:220311 Kengoshiduka 1.jpg|280px]] |imageCaption=Full view of the mound (2022) |location={{ill|Nara Prefecture|ja|奈良県}}{{ill|Asuka, Nara|ja|明日香村}} |coordinates={{coordinates|34|27|58.7|N|135|47|32.29|E|region:JP-29}} |type={{ill|Octagonal Kofun|ja|八角墳}} |Scale=Main mound diameter approx. 22m (including paved stone and gravel areas, 32m) |ConstructionPeriod=Mid {{ill|7th century|ja|7世紀}} to early {{ill|8th century|ja|8世紀}} |Occupant=(Hypothetical) {{ill|Empress Saimei|ja|斉明天皇}} (37th Emperor) |Artifacts=Lacquered coffin fragments, {{ill|Cloisonné|ja|七宝}} decorative fittings, molars |HistoricSite=National Historic Site: "Kengoshizuka Kofun and Kosotsukamikado Kofun" |TangibleCulturalProperty=Artifacts designated as National {{ill|Important Cultural Property (Japan)|ja|重要文化財}} |Map={{location map|Japan Nara|lat_deg=34|lat_min=27|lat_sec=58.7|lon_deg=135|lon_min=47|lon_sec=32.29|label=Kengoshizuka
Mausoleum|mark={{ill|Octagonal Kofun|ja|八角墳}}.svg|marksize=28|caption=|position=bottom|width=200|float=center}} }} '''Kengoshizuka Kofun''' is a [[Kofun]] in [[Asuka, Nara]] Japan.Tokuse, Takahiko, and Eriko Oka. "Life in Archaeological Sites and Settlements in Asuka Village as a Model Case for Managing Settlements Adjacent to Archaeological Sites: A Proposal for the Future of Saqqara." The journal of Center for the Global Study of Cultural Heritage and Culture 2 (2015): 5-20.{{cite book |title=Burial Mounds in Europe and Japan: Comparative and Contextual Perspectives |date=30 September 2018 |doi=10.2307/j.ctv1228gf7|s2cid=240193791 }} Specifically, it is an [[Octagonal Kofun]]. It is said to be the burial site of [[Empress Kōgyoku]].{{Cite web |title=Kengoshizuka Kofun Tumulus, Koshitsuka-gomon Kofun Tumulus |url=http://asuka-japan-heritage.jp/global/en/saimei/detail/kengosiduka_sa.html |access-date=2023-10-20 |website=Exploring the Footsteps of the Heroines of Asuka |language=en}}{{Cite news |date=2022-03-04 |title=Octagonal burial mound said to belong to ancient Japan empress reconstructed in Nara Pref. |language=en |work=Mainichi Daily News |url=https://mainichi.jp/english/articles/20220304/p2a/00m/0na/040000c |access-date=2023-10-20}} it was reconstructed and opened to the public on May 6 2022. This contrasts with other Imperial tombs such as the [[Mausoleum of Emperor Tenji]] which are closed to the public by the [[Imperial Household Agency]].{{Cite web |title=Gobyōyama Kofun (in Kyōto) - Passage Grave in Japan in Honshū |url=https://www.megalithic.co.uk/article.php?sid=33021 |access-date=2023-10-21 |website=The Megalithic Portal}} [[File:220311 Kengoshiduka 3.jpg|thumb|Entrance to the burial chamber]] ==overview== '''Kengoshizuka Kofun''' (牽牛子塚古墳) is a {{ill|Kofun|ja|古墳}} located in {{ill|Asuka, Nara|ja|明日香村}}, {{ill|Nara Prefecture|ja|奈良県}}, Japan. It is an {{ill|Octagonal Kofun|ja|八角墳}} and has been designated as a National Historic Site. The excavated artifacts from the site are designated as National Important Cultural Properties. The name "Kengoshizuka" includes the word "{{ill|Asagao|ja|アサガオ}}" ([[:en:Ipomoea_nil|Morning Glory]]), an alternate reading for "Kengoshi." The tumulus is also referred to as "Omae-zuka."[http://www.asukamura.jp/chosa_hokoku/kengoshizuka/kengoshizuka.html Kengoshizuka Kofun] Asuka Village Official Website Excavations conducted between 2009 and 2010 revealed that the tumulus was octagonal, strengthening its association with {{ill|Empress Saimei|ja|斉明天皇}}, mother of {{ill|Emperor Tenji|ja|天智天皇}} and {{ill|Emperor Tenmu|ja|天武天皇}}. Full restoration was completed in February 2022.Nara's Asuka Morning Glory Kofun fully restored, "Mainichi Shimbun," March 3, 2022, Osaka Morning Edition == location == The tumulus is located near the border of {{ill|Kashihara|ja|橿原市}} and lies at the stable, broad apex of a hill in {{ill|Asuka, Nara|ja|明日香村}}. Its summit reaches an elevation of 126.3 meters and is approximately 500 meters west of the {{ill|Iwayayama Kofun|ja|岩屋山古墳}}, another National Historic Site. == Exterior and Scale == The site was previously known for its unique internal structure, consisting of two hollowed chambers within a massive stone. This led to theories that it served as a combined tomb for Empress Saimei and her daughter {{ill|Princess Hashihito|ja|間人皇女}} (consort of {{ill|Emperor Kōtoku|ja|孝徳天皇}}). Excavations in 1977–1978 created measured diagrams based on surveys, and while it was initially reported as a circular tumulus,Ōtsuka, Hatsushige, and Kobayashi, Saburō (1982). *Dictionary of Kofun.* Tokyo: Tōkyodō Publishing, pp. 108-109. the possibility of an octagonal structure was also noted. From September 2009 to September 2010, academic excavations by the Asuka Village Board of Education confirmed the octagonal layout.[http://mainichi.jp/select/wadai/news/20100910k0000m040050000c.html Kengoshizuka Kofun: Confirmed as Octagonal Structure and Likely Burial Site of Empress Saimei.] "Mainichi Shimbun," September 9, 2010.[http://mainichi.jp/select/wadai/news/20100910k0000m040072000c.html Kengoshizuka Kofun: A 550-ton Stone Mausoleum Exhibiting Authority.] "Mainichi Shimbun," September 9, 2010.[http://www.jiji.com/jc/c?g=soc_30&k=2010090900686 Octagonal Mound Confirmed for Kengoshizuka Kofun: Further Evidence of Empress Saimei's Tomb.] "Jiji Press," September 9, 2010. The mound was found to be a triple-tiered octagonal tumulus standing approximately 4.5 meters tall, with the base measuring 22 meters across. Surrounding the mound is a paved stone structure with a similar octagonal shape, extending the total diameter to approximately 32 meters, including gravel layers. Hundreds of meticulously carved white tuff stones were uncovered, estimated to have originally numbered 7,200 and used to create a pyramid-like exterior.Asahi Shimbun, September 10, 2010. == Interior Structure == The interior is a {{ill|yokoguchi-style sekkaku|ja|横口式石槨|1=Side-entrance Sarcophagus Chamber}} (side-entry stone chamber), partially exposed as of 2009. The chamber is carved from a massive block of tuff weighing approximately 80 tons, sourced from [[:en:Mount_Nijō|Mount Nijō]] 15 kilometers away. The dimensions of the chamber are 5 meters wide, 3.5 meters deep, and 2.5 meters high, divided into two spaces by a central partition wall. The total weight of the stones used in the construction exceeds 550 tons. Transporting such massive stones over long distances required significant manpower, highlighting the power of the centralized state. == Excavated Artifacts == Artifacts include lacquered coffin fragments, gold-copper fittings with {{ill|Cloisonné|ja|七宝}} patterns, glass beads, and human molars believed to belong to Princess Hashihito. These were designated as National Important Cultural Properties in 1953.{{国指定文化財等データベース|201|9725|牽牛子塚古墳出土品}} == Cultural Significance == The Kofun's unique octagonal shape aligns it with other imperial tombs such as the {{ill|Dannotsuka Kofun|ja|段ノ塚古墳}} (tomb of {{ill|Emperor Jomei|ja|舒明天皇}}) and the {{ill|Noguchi Ouka Tomb|ja|野口王墓}} (joint tomb of {{ill|Emperor Tenmu|ja|天武天皇}} and {{ill|Empress Jitō|ja|持統天皇}}). This reinforces its probable identification as the tomb of Empress Saimei. == Adjacent Kofun == In December 2010, the Asuka Village Board of Education announced the discovery of a smaller kofun adjacent to Kengoshizuka Kofun. This nearby tomb, named {{ill|Kosotsukamikado Kofun|ja|越塚御門古墳}}, is hypothesized to be the tomb of Princess Ōta, Empress Saimei's granddaughter.[https://web.archive.org/web/20101211190601/http://www.yomiuri.co.jp/national/culture/news/20101209-OYT1T00770.htm Adjacent Tomb Likely Princess Ōta's Burial Site.] Yomiuri Shimbun, December 9, 2010. == Access == * Approximately 550 meters northwest of {{ill|Asuka Station|ja|飛鳥駅}} ({{ill|Kintetsu Yoshino Line|ja|近鉄吉野線}}). == References == {{Reflist}} == External Links == {{Commonscat|Kengoshizuka Kofun}} * [http://www.asukamura.jp/chosa_hokoku/kengoshizuka/kengoshizuka.html Kengoshizuka Kofun] - Asuka Village Official Website * {{国指定文化財等データベース|401|1945|牽牛子塚古墳・越塚御門古墳}} * {{国指定文化財等データベース|201|9725|大和国高市郡牽牛子塚古墳出土品}} {{afc comment|1=idk what to do with this because the wikipedia page was expanded heavily in a different direction on enwiki[[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 03:21, 14 February 2025 (UTC)}} {{Short description|Tomb of Empress Kōgyoku of Japan}}{{Expand Japanese}}{{Infobox ancient site |name=Kengoshizuka Kofun |image=[[File:220311 Kengoshiduka 1.jpg|280px]] |imageCaption=Full view of the mound (2022) |location={{ill|Nara Prefecture|ja|奈良県}}{{ill|Asuka, Nara|ja|明日香村}} |coordinates={{coordinates|34|27|58.7|N|135|47|32.29|E|region:JP-29}} |type={{ill|Octagonal Kofun|ja|八角墳}} |Scale=Main mound diameter approx. 22m (including paved stone and gravel areas, 32m) |ConstructionPeriod=Mid {{ill|7th century|ja|7世紀}} to early {{ill|8th century|ja|8世紀}} |Occupant=(Hypothetical) {{ill|Empress Saimei|ja|斉明天皇}} (37th Emperor) |Artifacts=Lacquered coffin fragments, {{ill|Cloisonné|ja|七宝}} decorative fittings, molars |HistoricSite=National Historic Site: "Kengoshizuka Kofun and Kosotsukamikado Kofun" |TangibleCulturalProperty=Artifacts designated as National {{ill|Important Cultural Property (Japan)|ja|重要文化財}} |Map={{location map|Japan Nara|lat_deg=34|lat_min=27|lat_sec=58.7|lon_deg=135|lon_min=47|lon_sec=32.29|label=Kengoshizuka
Mausoleum|mark={{ill|Octagonal Kofun|ja|八角墳}}.svg|marksize=28|caption=|position=bottom|width=200|float=center}} }} '''Kengoshizuka Kofun''' is a [[Kofun]] in [[Asuka, Nara]] Japan.Tokuse, Takahiko, and Eriko Oka. "Life in Archaeological Sites and Settlements in Asuka Village as a Model Case for Managing Settlements Adjacent to Archaeological Sites: A Proposal for the Future of Saqqara." The journal of Center for the Global Study of Cultural Heritage and Culture 2 (2015): 5-20.{{cite book |title=Burial Mounds in Europe and Japan: Comparative and Contextual Perspectives |date=30 September 2018 |doi=10.2307/j.ctv1228gf7|s2cid=240193791 }} Specifically, it is an [[Octagonal Kofun]]. It is said to be the burial site of [[Empress Kōgyoku]].{{Cite web |title=Kengoshizuka Kofun Tumulus, Koshitsuka-gomon Kofun Tumulus |url=http://asuka-japan-heritage.jp/global/en/saimei/detail/kengosiduka_sa.html |access-date=2023-10-20 |website=Exploring the Footsteps of the Heroines of Asuka |language=en}}{{Cite news |date=2022-03-04 |title=Octagonal burial mound said to belong to ancient Japan empress reconstructed in Nara Pref. |language=en |work=Mainichi Daily News |url=https://mainichi.jp/english/articles/20220304/p2a/00m/0na/040000c |access-date=2023-10-20}} it was reconstructed and opened to the public on May 6 2022. This contrasts with other Imperial tombs such as the [[Mausoleum of Emperor Tenji]] which are closed to the public by the [[Imperial Household Agency]].{{Cite web |title=Gobyōyama Kofun (in Kyōto) - Passage Grave in Japan in Honshū |url=https://www.megalithic.co.uk/article.php?sid=33021 |access-date=2023-10-21 |website=The Megalithic Portal}} [[File:220311 Kengoshiduka 3.jpg|thumb|Entrance to the burial chamber]] ==overview== '''Kengoshizuka Kofun''' (牽牛子塚古墳) is a {{ill|Kofun|ja|古墳}} located in {{ill|Asuka, Nara|ja|明日香村}}, {{ill|Nara Prefecture|ja|奈良県}}, Japan. It is an {{ill|Octagonal Kofun|ja|八角墳}} and has been designated as a National Historic Site. The excavated artifacts from the site are designated as National Important Cultural Properties. The name "Kengoshizuka" includes the word "{{ill|Asagao|ja|アサガオ}}" ([[:en:Ipomoea_nil|Morning Glory]]), an alternate reading for "Kengoshi." The tumulus is also referred to as "Omae-zuka."[http://www.asukamura.jp/chosa_hokoku/kengoshizuka/kengoshizuka.html Kengoshizuka Kofun] Asuka Village Official Website Excavations conducted between 2009 and 2010 revealed that the tumulus was octagonal, strengthening its association with {{ill|Empress Saimei|ja|斉明天皇}}, mother of {{ill|Emperor Tenji|ja|天智天皇}} and {{ill|Emperor Tenmu|ja|天武天皇}}. Full restoration was completed in February 2022.Nara's Asuka Morning Glory Kofun fully restored, "Mainichi Shimbun," March 3, 2022, Osaka Morning Edition == location == The tumulus is located near the border of {{ill|Kashihara|ja|橿原市}} and lies at the stable, broad apex of a hill in {{ill|Asuka, Nara|ja|明日香村}}. Its summit reaches an elevation of 126.3 meters and is approximately 500 meters west of the {{ill|Iwayayama Kofun|ja|岩屋山古墳}}, another National Historic Site. == Exterior and Scale == The site was previously known for its unique internal structure, consisting of two hollowed chambers within a massive stone. This led to theories that it served as a combined tomb for Empress Saimei and her daughter {{ill|Princess Hashihito|ja|間人皇女}} (consort of {{ill|Emperor Kōtoku|ja|孝徳天皇}}). Excavations in 1977–1978 created measured diagrams based on surveys, and while it was initially reported as a circular tumulus,Ōtsuka, Hatsushige, and Kobayashi, Saburō (1982). *Dictionary of Kofun.* Tokyo: Tōkyodō Publishing, pp. 108-109. the possibility of an octagonal structure was also noted. From September 2009 to September 2010, academic excavations by the Asuka Village Board of Education confirmed the octagonal layout.[http://mainichi.jp/select/wadai/news/20100910k0000m040050000c.html Kengoshizuka Kofun: Confirmed as Octagonal Structure and Likely Burial Site of Empress Saimei.] "Mainichi Shimbun," September 9, 2010.[http://mainichi.jp/select/wadai/news/20100910k0000m040072000c.html Kengoshizuka Kofun: A 550-ton Stone Mausoleum Exhibiting Authority.] "Mainichi Shimbun," September 9, 2010.[http://www.jiji.com/jc/c?g=soc_30&k=2010090900686 Octagonal Mound Confirmed for Kengoshizuka Kofun: Further Evidence of Empress Saimei's Tomb.] "Jiji Press," September 9, 2010. The mound was found to be a triple-tiered octagonal tumulus standing approximately 4.5 meters tall, with the base measuring 22 meters across. Surrounding the mound is a paved stone structure with a similar octagonal shape, extending the total diameter to approximately 32 meters, including gravel layers. Hundreds of meticulously carved white tuff stones were uncovered, estimated to have originally numbered 7,200 and used to create a pyramid-like exterior.Asahi Shimbun, September 10, 2010. == Interior Structure == The interior is a {{ill|yokoguchi-style sekkaku|ja|横口式石槨|1=Side-entrance Sarcophagus Chamber}} (side-entry stone chamber), partially exposed as of 2009. The chamber is carved from a massive block of tuff weighing approximately 80 tons, sourced from [[:en:Mount_Nijō|Mount Nijō]] 15 kilometers away. The dimensions of the chamber are 5 meters wide, 3.5 meters deep, and 2.5 meters high, divided into two spaces by a central partition wall. The total weight of the stones used in the construction exceeds 550 tons. Transporting such massive stones over long distances required significant manpower, highlighting the power of the centralized state. == Excavated Artifacts == Artifacts include lacquered coffin fragments, gold-copper fittings with {{ill|Cloisonné|ja|七宝}} patterns, glass beads, and human molars believed to belong to Princess Hashihito. These were designated as National Important Cultural Properties in 1953.{{国指定文化財等データベース|201|9725|牽牛子塚古墳出土品}} == Cultural Significance == The Kofun's unique octagonal shape aligns it with other imperial tombs such as the {{ill|Dannotsuka Kofun|ja|段ノ塚古墳}} (tomb of {{ill|Emperor Jomei|ja|舒明天皇}}) and the {{ill|Noguchi Ouka Tomb|ja|野口王墓}} (joint tomb of {{ill|Emperor Tenmu|ja|天武天皇}} and {{ill|Empress Jitō|ja|持統天皇}}). This reinforces its probable identification as the tomb of Empress Saimei. == Adjacent Kofun == In December 2010, the Asuka Village Board of Education announced the discovery of a smaller kofun adjacent to Kengoshizuka Kofun. This nearby tomb, named {{ill|Kosotsukamikado Kofun|ja|越塚御門古墳}}, is hypothesized to be the tomb of Princess Ōta, Empress Saimei's granddaughter.[https://web.archive.org/web/20101211190601/http://www.yomiuri.co.jp/national/culture/news/20101209-OYT1T00770.htm Adjacent Tomb Likely Princess Ōta's Burial Site.] Yomiuri Shimbun, December 9, 2010. == Access == * Approximately 550 meters northwest of {{ill|Asuka Station|ja|飛鳥駅}} ({{ill|Kintetsu Yoshino Line|ja|近鉄吉野線}}). == References == {{Reflist}} == External Links == {{afc comment|1=idk what to do with this because the wikipedia page was expanded heavily in a different direction on enwiki[[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 03:21, 14 February 2025 (UTC)}} {{Short description|Tomb of Empress Kōgyoku of Japan}}{{Expand Japanese}}{{Infobox ancient site |name=Kengoshizuka Kofun |image=[[File:220311 Kengoshiduka 1.jpg|280px]] |imageCaption=Full view of the mound (2022) |location={{ill|Nara Prefecture|ja|奈良県}}{{ill|Asuka, Nara|ja|明日香村}} |coordinates={{coordinates|34|27|58.7|N|135|47|32.29|E|region:JP-29}} |type={{ill|Octagonal Kofun|ja|八角墳}} |Scale=Main mound diameter approx. 22m (including paved stone and gravel areas, 32m) |ConstructionPeriod=Mid {{ill|7th century|ja|7世紀}} to early {{ill|8th century|ja|8世紀}} |Occupant=(Hypothetical) {{ill|Empress Saimei|ja|斉明天皇}} (37th Emperor) |Artifacts=Lacquered coffin fragments, {{ill|Cloisonné|ja|七宝}} decorative fittings, molars |HistoricSite=National Historic Site: "Kengoshizuka Kofun and Kosotsukamikado Kofun" |TangibleCulturalProperty=Artifacts designated as National {{ill|Important Cultural Property (Japan)|ja|重要文化財}} |Map={{location map|Japan Nara|lat_deg=34|lat_min=27|lat_sec=58.7|lon_deg=135|lon_min=47|lon_sec=32.29|label=Kengoshizuka
Mausoleum|mark={{ill|Octagonal Kofun|ja|八角墳}}.svg|marksize=28|caption=|position=bottom|width=200|float=center}} }} '''Kengoshizuka Kofun''' is a [[Kofun]] in [[Asuka, Nara]] Japan.Tokuse, Takahiko, and Eriko Oka. "Life in Archaeological Sites and Settlements in Asuka Village as a Model Case for Managing Settlements Adjacent to Archaeological Sites: A Proposal for the Future of Saqqara." The journal of Center for the Global Study of Cultural Heritage and Culture 2 (2015): 5-20.{{cite book |title=Burial Mounds in Europe and Japan: Comparative and Contextual Perspectives |date=30 September 2018 |doi=10.2307/j.ctv1228gf7|s2cid=240193791 }} Specifically, it is an [[Octagonal Kofun]]. It is said to be the burial site of [[Empress Kōgyoku]].{{Cite web |title=Kengoshizuka Kofun Tumulus, Koshitsuka-gomon Kofun Tumulus |url=http://asuka-japan-heritage.jp/global/en/saimei/detail/kengosiduka_sa.html |access-date=2023-10-20 |website=Exploring the Footsteps of the Heroines of Asuka |language=en}}{{Cite news |date=2022-03-04 |title=Octagonal burial mound said to belong to ancient Japan empress reconstructed in Nara Pref. |language=en |work=Mainichi Daily News |url=https://mainichi.jp/english/articles/20220304/p2a/00m/0na/040000c |access-date=2023-10-20}} it was reconstructed and opened to the public on May 6 2022. This contrasts with other Imperial tombs such as the [[Mausoleum of Emperor Tenji]] which are closed to the public by the [[Imperial Household Agency]].{{Cite web |title=Gobyōyama Kofun (in Kyōto) - Passage Grave in Japan in Honshū |url=https://www.megalithic.co.uk/article.php?sid=33021 |access-date=2023-10-21 |website=The Megalithic Portal}} [[File:220311 Kengoshiduka 3.jpg|thumb|Entrance to the burial chamber]] ==overview== '''Kengoshizuka Kofun''' (牽牛子塚古墳) is a {{ill|Kofun|ja|古墳}} located in {{ill|Asuka, Nara|ja|明日香村}}, {{ill|Nara Prefecture|ja|奈良県}}, Japan. It is an {{ill|Octagonal Kofun|ja|八角墳}} and has been designated as a National Historic Site. The excavated artifacts from the site are designated as National Important Cultural Properties. The name "Kengoshizuka" includes the word "{{ill|Asagao|ja|アサガオ}}" ([[:en:Ipomoea_nil|Morning Glory]]), an alternate reading for "Kengoshi." The tumulus is also referred to as "Omae-zuka."[http://www.asukamura.jp/chosa_hokoku/kengoshizuka/kengoshizuka.html Kengoshizuka Kofun] Asuka Village Official Website Excavations conducted between 2009 and 2010 revealed that the tumulus was octagonal, strengthening its association with {{ill|Empress Saimei|ja|斉明天皇}}, mother of {{ill|Emperor Tenji|ja|天智天皇}} and {{ill|Emperor Tenmu|ja|天武天皇}}. Full restoration was completed in February 2022.Nara's Asuka Morning Glory Kofun fully restored, "Mainichi Shimbun," March 3, 2022, Osaka Morning Edition == location == The tumulus is located near the border of {{ill|Kashihara|ja|橿原市}} and lies at the stable, broad apex of a hill in {{ill|Asuka, Nara|ja|明日香村}}. Its summit reaches an elevation of 126.3 meters and is approximately 500 meters west of the {{ill|Iwayayama Kofun|ja|岩屋山古墳}}, another National Historic Site. == Exterior and Scale == The site was previously known for its unique internal structure, consisting of two hollowed chambers within a massive stone. This led to theories that it served as a combined tomb for Empress Saimei and her daughter {{ill|Princess Hashihito|ja|間人皇女}} (consort of {{ill|Emperor Kōtoku|ja|孝徳天皇}}). Excavations in 1977–1978 created measured diagrams based on surveys, and while it was initially reported as a circular tumulus,Ōtsuka, Hatsushige, and Kobayashi, Saburō (1982). *Dictionary of Kofun.* Tokyo: Tōkyodō Publishing, pp. 108-109. the possibility of an octagonal structure was also noted. From September 2009 to September 2010, academic excavations by the Asuka Village Board of Education confirmed the octagonal layout.[http://mainichi.jp/select/wadai/news/20100910k0000m040050000c.html Kengoshizuka Kofun: Confirmed as Octagonal Structure and Likely Burial Site of Empress Saimei.] "Mainichi Shimbun," September 9, 2010.[http://mainichi.jp/select/wadai/news/20100910k0000m040072000c.html Kengoshizuka Kofun: A 550-ton Stone Mausoleum Exhibiting Authority.] "Mainichi Shimbun," September 9, 2010.[http://www.jiji.com/jc/c?g=soc_30&k=2010090900686 Octagonal Mound Confirmed for Kengoshizuka Kofun: Further Evidence of Empress Saimei's Tomb.] "Jiji Press," September 9, 2010. The mound was found to be a triple-tiered octagonal tumulus standing approximately 4.5 meters tall, with the base measuring 22 meters across. Surrounding the mound is a paved stone structure with a similar octagonal shape, extending the total diameter to approximately 32 meters, including gravel layers. Hundreds of meticulously carved white tuff stones were uncovered, estimated to have originally numbered 7,200 and used to create a pyramid-like exterior.Asahi Shimbun, September 10, 2010. == Interior Structure == The interior is a {{ill|yokoguchi-style sekkaku|ja|横口式石槨|1=Side-entrance Sarcophagus Chamber}} (side-entry stone chamber), partially exposed as of 2009. The chamber is carved from a massive block of tuff weighing approximately 80 tons, sourced from [[:en:Mount_Nijō|Mount Nijō]] 15 kilometers away. The dimensions of the chamber are 5 meters wide, 3.5 meters deep, and 2.5 meters high, divided into two spaces by a central partition wall. The total weight of the stones used in the construction exceeds 550 tons. Transporting such massive stones over long distances required significant manpower, highlighting the power of the centralized state. == Excavated Artifacts == Artifacts include lacquered coffin fragments, gold-copper fittings with {{ill|Cloisonné|ja|七宝}} patterns, glass beads, and human molars believed to belong to Princess Hashihito. These were designated as National Important Cultural Properties in 1953.{{国指定文化財等データベース|201|9725|牽牛子塚古墳出土品}} == Cultural Significance == The Kofun's unique octagonal shape aligns it with other imperial tombs such as the {{ill|Dannotsuka Kofun|ja|段ノ塚古墳}} (tomb of {{ill|Emperor Jomei|ja|舒明天皇}}) and the {{ill|Noguchi Ouka Tomb|ja|野口王墓}} (joint tomb of {{ill|Emperor Tenmu|ja|天武天皇}} and {{ill|Empress Jitō|ja|持統天皇}}). This reinforces its probable identification as the tomb of Empress Saimei. == Adjacent Kofun == In December 2010, the Asuka Village Board of Education announced the discovery of a smaller kofun adjacent to Kengoshizuka Kofun. This nearby tomb, named {{ill|Kosotsukamikado Kofun|ja|越塚御門古墳}}, is hypothesized to be the tomb of Princess Ōta, Empress Saimei's granddaughter.[https://web.archive.org/web/20101211190601/http://www.yomiuri.co.jp/national/culture/news/20101209-OYT1T00770.htm Adjacent Tomb Likely Princess Ōta's Burial Site.] Yomiuri Shimbun, December 9, 2010. == Access == * Approximately 550 meters northwest of {{ill|Asuka Station|ja|飛鳥駅}} ({{ill|Kintetsu Yoshino Line|ja|近鉄吉野線}}). == References == {{Reflist}} == External Links ==
